chapters.title: Info
chapters.intro: An introduction to nuclear reactions, nuclear reactors and their design.

pages.title: Nuclear Physics
pages.text: Nuclear reactions fall into two main types, fission and fusion. Each of these works off of Einstein's theory of relativity to generate energy from mass - E = mc^2. This energy is released as heat or as a speeding neutron. Because the value of c (the speed of light) is extremely large - 300 million meters per second - the amount of energy released is often very large, even though the mass consumption is tiny.

pages.title: Nuclear Fission
pages.text: In nuclear fission, a heavy atom, such as that of uranium or plutonium, is impacted with an extra neutron. This destabilizes it, and the atom soon splits into two others, releasing a large amount of energy in the process. This reaction also releases three more neutrons, which can impact three more atoms and trigger a chain reaction. The two resultant atoms are usually unwanted and hazardous waste products.

pages.title: Nuclear Fusion
pages.text: In nuclear fusion, two light atoms, usually hydrogen, are forced together under extreme heat and pressure until they join together. Some mass is lost in this process, releasing heat and a speeding neutron. This neutron carries a large amount of the energy from this reaction and must be captured to regain that energy. Unlike fission, fusion cannot create a chain reaction, and produces no waste, but it is much more difficult to accomplish. Most artificial fusion reactors use two hydrogen isotopes, deuterium and tritium.

pages.title: Nuclear Power Basics
pages.text: Nuclear power plants work in fundamentally the same way as most others; the nuclear reaction generates heat, which is eventually used to boil water into steam. This steam drives a turbine and generates shaft power. Nuclear fuel is consumed rather slowly compared to most others, but it is often difficult to produce and its after-effects are often difficult to dispose of.

pages.title: Uranium Enrichment
pages.text: Uranium comes in two main varieties, U235 and U238. Only U235 is immediately useful for nuclear power, but it makes up less than 1%% of all uranium, with the rest being U238. For this reason, uranium is 'enriched', where the concentration of U235 is increased to usable levels. The U238 left over, sometimes termed 'depleted uranium', can be bombarded with neutrons to convert it into Pu239, a form of plutonium also usable in fission reactors, though with more risk and worse waste products. Depleted uranium can also be used to make high-density objects.

pages.title: Meltdowns
pages.text: If a reactor gets too hot, it will start to boil off its coolant and emit large quantities of smoke and steam. Hotter still, and it may cause the water molecules to break apart, resulting in a large accumulation of hydrogen gas. Because hydrogen gas is flammable, it can often result in an explosion that sends pieces of the reactor in all directions. Additionally, the fuel and steel structure of the fuel core itself will soften, melt and mix into a lavalike fluid called "corium", which is intensely radioactive. Meltdowns spread extreme radiation over a fairly large area.

pages.title: Radiation
pages.text: Radioactivity is a dangerous property of many nuclear materials, as it will severely poison living things. Low-level radioactivity is not immediately lethal, but it can bring about unpleasant effects such as dizziness and nausea. Higher levels of radioactivity, such as those left behind after a nuclear meltdown, will kill in fairly short order. Radioactivity leaves a distinctive mark on the land, killing plants, grass, and and animals alike. Radiation cannot be cleaned manually, but will gradually decay over time, and can be washed away by rain.

pages.title: Shielding
pages.text: Most reactors fire out high-energy neutrons that can harm or kill living things, and to this end it is almost universally advisable to shield such a reactor. Additionally, should a meltdown occur, proper shielding can limit both structural damage and the spread of lethal levels of radiation. Only a few block types are effective in this regard.

pages.title: Structures
pages.text: Nuclear reactors and their parts are often large, far larger than the cubic meter in which most machines will fit. Additionally, they are often comprised of many individual parts which only form a coherent whole in a specific arrangement.

chapters.title: Processing
chapters.intro: These machines are used to process existing materials into ones needed for making functional reactors.

pages.title: Uranium Processor
pages.text: The uranium processor dissolves fluorite in water to make hydrofluoric acid, and then dissolves raw uranium in the acid to make uranium hexafluoride gas. This gas is used in the uranium enrichment process.
pages.notes:
Does not require power
Requires a water supply

pages.title: Isotope Centrifuge
pages.text: The isotope centrifuge uses a very high rotational speed to separate the different isotopes of uranium, and will produce a mixture of depleted uranium dust and enriched uranium dust. The latter is far less common due to the rarity of U235.
pages.notes:
Minimum Speed: 262144 rad/s
Power Input: Bottom
UF6 Input: Top

pages.title: Electrolyzer
pages.text: The electrolyzer uses electrical discharges to decompose materials into their constituents, such as salt into sodium and chlorine or water into hydrogen and oxygen. The heavier of the products is drawn from the bottom, while the lighter is drawn from the top. Note that solids must be melted down before they are able to be processed.
pages.notes: Required temperature to melt salt: 801C

pages.title: Fluid Synthesizer
pages.text: The synthesizer is primarily used to make ammonia, which is a more effective working fluid in reactors than water. To do this, it requires water, ammonium chloride, and quicklime. It can also process a few other fluids.
pages.notes: Ammonia Synthesis Temperature: 220C

pages.title: Neutron Irradiation Chamber
pages.text: The neutron irradiation chamber converts deuterium to tritium by bombarding it with neutrons. This machine is placed in the core of a reactor, where it will absorb some neutrons that hit it and convert the stored deuterium.
pages.notes:
Deuterium Input: Top
Tritium Output: Bottom

chapters.title: Power Generation
chapters.intro: These machines harness the power of a nuclear reactor, and work together to convert it into usable shaft power.

pages.title: Steam Boiler
pages.text: The boiler absorbs heat from the surrounding machines and uses it to boil the internal liquid into steam. Note that if the steam is not drawn away and allowed to accumulate, the boiler will eventually lose the ability to boil more liquid and fail to draw away heat from the reactor. This usually results in a meltdown. Also, if the temperature rises above 650C when the boiler is full of ammonia, the ammonia will ignite and detonate.
pages.notes:
Liquid Input: Bottom:
Steam Output: Top

pages.title: Steam Line
pages.text: Steam lines transport the steam away from the reactor to a turbine. Note that the steam line has an infinite capacity and thus breaking it may result in a loss of a large amount of stored energy.
pages.notes: Infinite capacity

pages.title: Steam Grate
pages.text: The steam grate takes in steam from steam lines and releases it into the world. The steam will then rise until it hits a blockage, where it will spread out. Ideally, the steam should rise directly into a turbine so that its energy can be extracted.
pages.notes:
Steam Output: Top
Max Ouput: 1 block per tick (20 blocks/s)

pages.title: Turbine
pages.text: The turbine extracts the energy from steam, which moves along its length. The turbine will gradually accelerate as it receives steam, and its torque will be proportional to the amount of steam flowing through. Note that turbines, especially if rotating rapidly, are extremely fragile. The turbine will not run if its blades are obstructed.
pages.notes:
Max Speed: 65536 rad/s
Max Torque: 32768 Nm
Risks: Blade breakage due to collisions with objects
Turbines require lubrication

pages.title: Condenser
pages.text: The condenser will recollect steam blocks and convert it back into liquid for reuse in the nuclear reactor. Because the pressure is extremely low, this liquid must be repressurized before it can be used. While it may not be terribly economical to reclaim water-based steam, ammonia is sufficiently expensive that reclamation is well worth the cost.
pages.notes: Liquid Output: Top

pages.title: Heat Exchanger
pages.text: The heat exchanger takes hot fluid in the top and cools it down, transferring the fluid's heat into any adjacent machinery, including standard boilers. This machine requires power to force the fluid through, and the fluid can be drawn out the sides.
pages.notes:
Power Input: Bottom:
Required Power: 8192W
Required Speed: 512 rad/s

pages.title: Pressurizer
pages.text: The pressurizer repressurizes the low-pressure water or ammonia so that it can be reused in the reactor, thus completing the thermodynamic cycle. Note that this is a centrifugal compressor.
pages.notes:
Minimum Power: 16384W
Minimum Torque: 1024 Nm
Liquid Input: Top
Liquid Output: Side
Power Input: Bottom

pages.title: Turbine Generator
pages.text: The generator convers shaft power directly from a turbine into other forms of power for ease of transport or use in other mods. Note that it is a multiblock that must be directly connected to the turbine. Also be aware that the extreme power supply this generator provides exceeds the capacities of many transport systems.
pages.notes:
Converted Output: Back
Can be mode-switched with the screwdriver

pages.title: High-Pressure Turbine
pages.text: The high-pressure turbine runs off of steam directly from the lines thanks to a built-in steam injection system, allowing it to run more efficiently and generate far more power. Due to the greatly increased size of this turbine, it requires far more steam to operate, and can be built to seven stages instead of five. This turbine also has a housing to prevent damage. Low-pressure liquid can be collected with reservoirs or BC tanks below the back of the turbine.
pages.notes:
Max Speed: 131072 rad/s
Can be disabled with a redstone input to any of the injector blocks

chapters.title: HTGR
chapters.intro: These are the components to a High-Temperature Gas Reactor (HTGR).

pages.title: Pebble Bed Reactor Core
pages.text: The pebble bed reactor core is the fuel unit for a pebble bed reactor. Load it up with fuel pellets, and it will undergo spontaneous fission and generate heat. This heat is best transferred to a carbon dioxide heat exchanger.

pages.title: Carbon Dioxide Heat Exchanger
pages.text: The CO2 Heat Exchanger absorbs heat from a pebble bed reactor and transfers it into the carbon dioxide pumped in. The hot carbon dioxide can be drawn out the top and fed into a heat exchanger.
pages.notes: Must reach 800C to emit hot carbon dioxide

chapters.title: Fission
chapters.intro: These are the components to a standard boiling-water fission reactor.

pages.title: Fuel Core
pages.text: The fuel core stores the nuclear fuel and is the source of all nuclear reactions and heat generation. When loaded, the core will periodically emit neutrons, which can impact other fuel cores. If those cores are also loaded, there is a chance that they will undergo fission, releasing three more neutrons and some heat, and consume some fuel. They will also gradually accumulate waste, which will hamper their ability to undergo fission. If the fuel core gets too hot, it will begin smoking, releasing hydrogen gas, and will eventually melt and release large amounts of radiation.
pages.notes:
Neutron Emission: Any horizontal direction
Max Temperature: 1800C

pages.title: Control Rod
pages.text: The control rod allows you to manipulate the rate of a nuclear reaction by intercepting neutrons that could otherwise trigger more fission events. Control rods can be retracted or inserted - they are inserted by default - when commanded by a reactor CPU. They also can be dropped into place in the case of an emergency, a so-called "SCRAM" event.

pages.title: Coolant Cell
pages.text: Coolant cells draw away heat from the reactor. Note that this heat is essentially wasted, as it does not create any steam or useful energy. However, coolant cells are vital for distributing heat and stabilizing the temperature of larger reactors.

pages.title: Central Control
pages.text: The reactor CPU can be used to manage the operation of a nuclear reactor. It allows you to manipulate each control rod individually, or all at once. It also will sense the temperature of the surroundings and will trigger a SCRAM if the temperature gets too high, preventing a meltdown. Note that much as in a real reactor, if the CPU loses power for any reason, the control rods will all fall into place, likely stopping the nuclear reaction.
pages.notes: Power Per Control Rod: 1024W

pages.title: Forced Fission Chamber
pages.text: The forced fission chamber is used to bombard nuclear waste with neutrons to encourage it to fragment into products which are more easily disposed of than the original isotopes.
pages.notes: Operates most efficiently around 400C and with fast neutrons (if enabled)

chapters.title: Breeder
chapters.intro: These are the components to a sodium-cooled breeder reactor, or "liquid-metal fast breeder reactor" (LMFBR).

pages.title: Breeder Reactor Core
pages.text: The breeder reactor core behaves much like the normal fuel core, but can only accept breeder reactor fuel, and is the only type of reactor core that can be used in a breeder reactor. They heat up somewhat faster than normal uranium-fueled cores.
pages.notes:
Neutron Emission: Any horizontal direction
Max Temperature: 900C

pages.title: Sodium Heater
pages.text: The sodium heater will, much like a steam boiler, accumulate heat from the surroundings and heat up liquid pumped through it. However, it only accepts molten sodium and will output hot molten sodium once its temperature reaches 300 degrees. This hot molten sodium is usable in a heat exchanger.
pages.notes:
Sodium Input: Bottom
Hot Sodium Output: Top

chapters.title: Thorium
chapters.intro: These are the components to a liquid-fueled thorium reactor. These are fission reactors, but they are markedly different from other designs.

pages.title: Thorium Fuel Core
pages.text: Thorium reactor cores use molten thorium fuel salts (Thorium-enriched FLiBe) to generate electricity. Rather unique compared to other fission reactors, they are not self-sufficient and require heat and neutron flux in order to start. Additionally, the temperature-dependent neutron fertility means that as the temperature rises, they become less reactive, as a natural safeguard. The thorium fuel cycle also produces less waste than that of uranium.

pages.title: Fuel Dump Valve
pages.text: In the event of exceeding a critical temperature of 1100C, a thorium reactor will trigger an emergency fuel dump in order to avoid a meltdown. This can cause a radiation leak, and is to be avoided if possible.
pages.notes: Placed below the fuel column, and will trigger automatically to perform a dump

chapters.title: Fusion
chapters.intro: These are the components to a Tokamak fusion reactor.

pages.title: Hydrogen Preheater
pages.text: The hydrogen preheater uses the beam from the heat ray to heat a mixture of deuterium and tritium into a plasma usable in the fusion reactor. Note that it must be contained in a proper heater unit multiblock structure, and must be in the path of a heat ray beam.
pages.notes:
Plasma Temperature: 150000000C
Hydrogen Input: Any horizontal side
Plasma Output: Top

pages.title: Fusion Plasma Injector
pages.text: The plasma injector actually injects the fusion plasma into the tokamak reactor. Note that it must be contained in a proper multiblock structure.

pages.title: Toroid Magnet
pages.text: The toroidal magnets are the main component of the tokamak reactor, and contain the plasma into a narrow beam in their center. In order to function properly, they must be placed and rotated correctly, and kept very cold.
pages.notes: Can not be placed on flat ground due to large size

pages.title: Solenoid Magnet
pages.text: The solenoid magnet is the other main component of the tokamak reactor. It bends the plasma beam into a circle, allowing it to be contained and to reach the critical density for fusion to take place. If this magnet is not functional, the plasma beam will shoot off in a random direction. The solenoid is another large multiblock, and requires power to rotate.
pages.notes:
Minimum Speed: 256 rad/s
Minimum Torque: 32768 Nm
Maximum Speed: 8192 rad/s

pages.title: Neutron Absorber
pages.text: Neutron absorbers intercept neutrons and turn their kinetic energy into heat. Much like a heat exchanger, this heat can be transferred into adjacent machines.

chapters.title: Utility
chapters.intro: These machines are often required alongside the actual reactor, to produce or transport materials or to otherwise aid the reactors.

pages.title: Gas Collector
pages.text: The gas collector collects carbon dioxide from a furnace burning coal or wood. This carbon dioxide is used as the working fluid in high-temperature gas reactors.

pages.title: Gas Duct
pages.text: Gas Ducts are used to transport gas, and are made of clay so as not to react with corrosive gases like hydrofluoric acid and uranium hexafluoride.

pages.title: Magnetic Containment Pipe
pages.text: Magnetic containment pipes are used to transport extremely hot gases. They use a magnetic field to keep the contents away from the walls, as the pipe would otherwise melt. Note that an electrical charge must be applied to the pipe for it to work.
pages.notes: Requires charge from a Van De Graaff

pages.title: Centrifugal Fluid Extractor
pages.text: The fluid extractor, when submerged in and surrounded by source blocks of a fluid, can centrifuge it and obtain trace quantities of another fluid that was mixed in. For example, heavy water can be centrifuged out of the bottom of oceans (below y=45 and with at least 16m of water above), or molten lithium can be skimmed off the surface of lava.
pages.notes:
Minimum Power: 65536W
Minimum Torque: 512 Nm

pages.title: Spent Fuel Container
pages.text: The spent fuel container is the first disposal unit for nuclear waste. When placed in this container, the more radioactive nuclear waste with shorter half-lives will decay and generate heat and neutrons in the process. To keep the container cool, and to provide radiation shielding, it must be submerged underwater.

pages.title: Nuclear Waste Disposal Drum
pages.text: Longer-lived nuclear waste which will not decay in the spent fuel container must be placed in a waste disposal drum, where it may be safely stored underground indefinitely without risk of overheating or a radiation leak. Note that being in close proximity to a loaded container is still extremely dangerous. Waste with half-lives shorter than six years cannot be safely stored in this machine, as they generate too much heat.

pages.title: Neutron Reflector
pages.text: The neutron reflector has a chance of reflecting neutrons back in the direction from which they impacted the reflector. This allows for greater reactor efficiency by reusing a portion of the neutrons. Unreflected neutrons have a chance to be absorbed.

pages.title: Turbine Dynamometer
pages.text: The turbine dynamometer measures the speed of a turbine. It is placed below the body of a turbine, and will, with the aid of a redstone comparator, output a signal level corresponding to the turbine's speed as a fraction of its maximum speed.
pages.notes:
Must be placed below the turbine with a clear view above
Redstone signal level (Normal Turbine): (Speed/65536)*15
Redstone signal level (High-Pressure Turbine): (Speed/131072)*15

pages.title: Tokamak Blueprint Highlighter
pages.text: The tokamak blueprint highligher provides a general outline of the various parts of a tokamak fusion reactor to help with correctly placing and rotating the various components.

pages.title: Turbine Flywheel
pages.text: The turbine flywheel stabilizes the power output of a low-pressure turbine.

pages.title: Steam Diffuser
pages.text: The steam diffuser takes hot, high-pressure steam from a reactor boiler and expands and cools it to more conventional lower-pressure steam for use in conventional steam turbines designed for use with coal boilers.

pages.title: Solar Tower Sodium Cycler
pages.text: The Sodium Cycler allows you to use molten sodium instead of water in the solar tower, which greatly increases its power output and efficiency.
pages.notes: Two units must be stacked on top of the tower to function

pages.title: Solar Tower Sodium Heat Exchanger
pages.text: The Sodium Heat Exchanger allows you to get hot molten sodium out of a solar plant instead of direct shaft power. Though this is more complex, the power output is substantially larger.
pages.notes:
Placed below the tower column
Requires 65536W at 2048 rad/s

chapters.title: Tools
chapters.intro: These tools are useful to those working with nuclear reactors.

pages.title: Radiation Goggles
pages.text: Radiation Goggles allows radiation to become visible, allowing for easier avoidance and potential cleanup.

pages.title: Reactor CPU Remote Control
pages.text: The CPU remote is a way to control the CPU of a fission reactor at a distance, without having to enter the reactor itself.

pages.title: Geiger Counter
pages.text: The geiger counter can detect radiation, and will click more intensely as radiation levels rise.

pages.title: Radiation Cleanup Tool
pages.text: The radiation cleaning tool sprays water over an area to wash away radioactive particles, slowly cleaning it of radiation.

chapters.title: Resources
chapters.intro: These items are crucial in the operation of nuclear reactors.

pages.title: Fluorite Crystal
pages.text: Fluorite is a crystal that occurs naturally in rock. Fluorite comes in various colors, but all will fluoresce (give off light) in the presence of neutrons or radation, allowing them to be used as a crude geiger counter. Fluorite has a large concentration of fluorine, which is useful for making hydrofluoric acid during the uranium enrichment process.

pages.title: Uranium Fuel Pellet
pages.text: Uranium fuel pellets are the fuel source for a standard fission reactor. They are gradually consumed, and will eventually turn into depleted uranium when the U235 component in them is depleted.

pages.title: Depleted Uranium
pages.text: Depleted uranium is not useful as nuclear fuel on its own, but it can be converted into plutonium, which is.

pages.title: Nuclear Waste
pages.text: Nuclear waste is an extremely dangerous by-product of nuclear fission. It will accumulate in fuel cores and pollute the reactor, and therefore must be removed and properly disposed of. Held in hand or left in the world, its radioactivity will gradually poison the surroundings.

pages.title: Plutonium Fuel Pellet
pages.text: Plutonium is an alternate, artificial fuel for nuclear fission reactors. Plutonium is extremely dangerous and more volatile than uranium, and must be used and handled with extreme care.

pages.title: Breeder Reactor Fuel
pages.text: Breeder reactors require a special kind of fuel - standard enriched uranium wrapped in a layer of depleted uranium. Over time, the reactor's neutrons will convert this into plutonium.

pages.title: Permanent Magnet
pages.text: Magnets are used to manipulate the path of electrically charged things like plasma, and are used in great quantities in fusion reactors.

pages.title: TRISO Fuel Pellet
pages.text: Raw uranium can be powdered and mixed with graphite to create fuel pellets. These pellets are the fuel for a High-Temperature Gas Reactor.

pages.title: Depleted TRISO Fuel
pages.text: Like normal uranium fuel, fuel pellets eventually are depleted and no longer useful.
